newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia to decide on De Beers deal April 15.
newsitem.headline: Russia to decide on De Beers deal April 15.

text.p: Russia will decide on April 15 whether to sign a stalled gem trade deal with De Beers, a spokesman for gem producing company Almazy Rossii-Sakha, or ARS, which is De Beers' negotiating partner, said on Thursday.
"(First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly) Chubais has said the decision will be taken on April 15," ARS spokesman Valentin Logunov told Reuters.
"I don't think there will be any cardinal, principle changes to the trade deal," Lugunov said, referring to a draft trade agreement struck last year.
He said that if the deal were approved, the necessary presidential decrees and government orders authorising the trade arrangement could be signed one to two weeks later.

Logunov also said De Beers had bought some of ARS's $108 million sales of rough gems in Russia in February, but he said the South African giant was not able to export the stones because of Russian government delays in resolving export quota issues, which are part of the stalled deal.
De Beers, frustrated at Moscow's inability to communicate its position on a draft trade agreement submitted to the cabinet in October 1996, stopped buying gems from Russia at the end of last year.
The February purchase would have been De Beers's first buy of Russian rough gems on Russian territory since then.

Logunov said quarrels between Moscow and the diamond-producing republic of Sakha (Yakutia), where ARS is based, over what role the region should play in mining and sales had helped delay the agreement.

A De Beers delegation, headed by Gary Ralfe, director of the group's London-based Central Selling Organisation, or CSO, was in town for talks with ARS president Vyacheslav Shtyrov and other officials, Logunov said.
"The talks are in the form of working consultations and are about bilateral relations between ARS and De Beers," he said.
ARS March sales of rough gems had totalled only $27 million as of March 20, he said, adding that most, if not all, of the sales were to Russian cutters and polishers.
The CSO controls about three quarters of the world's $4.5 billion-a-year trade in uncut diamonds, and Russia accounts for about 20 percent of annual CSO sales.
